title: Prudential-HCL Venture Becomes India's Eighth Standalone Health Insurer and Starts Operations
summary: Prudential HCL Health Insurance received its IRDAI registration on July 1 and announced on August 20 that it has begun operations with an AI-enabled, direct-to-consumer model alongside agents.
description:
India's insurance regulator has registered a new standalone health insurer backed by the UK-listed Prudential plc and India's HCL Group. This article was first published in early August and has been updated on October 13, 2026 with the latest confirmed details, including the company's formal start of operations. According to Asia Insurance Post's report of July 1, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India granted Prudential HCL Health Insurance Limited a Certificate of Registration to carry on health insurance business. That takes the number of standalone health insurers in India to eight and was the regulator's third new insurance registration of calendar 2026.

The ownership is a 70:30 joint venture. Prudential plc holds 70% through a subsidiary, and Vama Sundari Investments, the HCL Group vehicle, holds the remaining 30%. The venture was announced in March 2025, so the registration closes a process that took more than a year. Prudential has named Amit Dave as managing director and chief executive, described as CEO designate in the August announcement, and Abhishek Saraf as chief operating officer. The amount of capital invested has not been disclosed in the sources reviewed.

On August 20 Prudential announced that the insurer, which will operate as Prudential Health India, had commenced operations. The company describes a digital-first, service-led model aimed at making health insurance simpler to understand, buy and use. It plans an omnichannel approach that combines personal advice through an agency network with an AI-enabled direct-to-consumer platform, and it points to access to more than 12,000 hospitals, digital tools for choosing cover and managing policies, and preventive health and support services. The announcement did not name launch cities, list specific products or give prices, so potential customers should not expect a detailed product catalogue until the insurer files and markets its plans.

The market it is entering is large. Prudential cites the General Insurance Council of India as estimating that India's health insurance market produced about US$16 billion in gross written premium in fiscal 2026, and attributes demand to rising incomes, favourable demographics and growing awareness of health protection. Naveen Tahilyani, Prudential's regional chief executive for several Asian and African markets, described India as a strategically important market for the group. Amit Dave referred to the government's "Insurance for All by 2047" goal. Shikhar Malhotra of Vama Sundari said HCL's entry into health insurance is a natural extension of its capabilities. Prudential also said in May that it is seeking a 75% stake in Bharti Life, in addition to its existing life insurance and asset management joint ventures in India.

What is a standalone health insurer, and why does the category exist? In India, general insurers sell motor, property, travel and health policies together, while standalone health insurers are licensed to sell only health, personal accident and travel cover. Regulators created the category to encourage companies that specialise in health and to deepen penetration in a country where many households still pay for treatment out of pocket. The practical difference for consumers is focus: a standalone insurer has no motor or property portfolio to manage, and its entire performance depends on health claims, hospital relationships and customer service.

For a prospective buyer, a new insurer brings both opportunities and questions. On the positive side, new entrants often compete on service and technology, offer simpler policy documents and may provide features such as wellness rewards or digital claims tracking. They can also push established insurers to improve. On the other side, a new company has no claim settlement history, no track record on how it treats disputed claims and a hospital network that may still be growing. The 12,000-hospital figure is a company statement, and what matters to an individual is whether the hospitals near them are included for cashless treatment.

Before buying a plan from any health insurer, whether new or established, there are practical checks. Confirm the waiting periods for pre-existing conditions and specific procedures, because these differ widely between plans. Look at room-rent limits, co-payment clauses and sub-limits, which can reduce a payout even when the headline sum insured looks high. Check the claim settlement ratio and the number of days it takes to settle claims once the insurer has published them, and read the IRDAI disclosures that insurers are required to make. Ask about portability, which lets you move your policy to another insurer without losing accumulated benefits such as waiting-period credits. Finally, compare the premium with equivalent cover from at least two other insurers, since price differences for the same sum insured can be significant.

The entry also says something about where Indian insurance is heading. Regulators have been pushing for wider coverage and more competition, and global insurers are building local platforms rather than relying only on partnerships. If the Prudential-HCL venture delivers on its digital promises, customers could gain simpler onboarding and quicker claims. If it struggles, the lesson will be that distribution and hospital relationships are as important as technology. In either case, the first full year of reported numbers will show how quickly it can build a book of business.

For now, the confirmed facts are limited: the registration, the ownership, the leadership and the start of operations. Anything beyond that, including products, premium rates and claim performance, will become clear only as the insurer launches and files its plans. Readers considering a purchase should wait for official product documents and verify them on the company's website and IRDAI's public disclosures.
image_alt: Healthcare professional using a tablet to review patient information (illustrative)
key_points: IRDAI granted Prudential HCL Health Insurance Limited a Certificate of Registration on July 1, 2026, making it India's eighth standalone health insurer and the regulator's third registration of the year.
Prudential plc holds 70% through a subsidiary and HCL Group's Vama Sundari Investments holds 30%; the joint venture was announced in March 2025.
On August 20, Prudential said the insurer had commenced operations, with a digital-first model combining agents and an AI-enabled direct-to-consumer platform.
The company cites a network of more than 12,000 hospitals and an Indian health insurance market of about US$16 billion in gross written premium in FY2026, per the General Insurance Council.
Amit Dave is the managing director and CEO designate; the insurer has not published product prices or the capital invested.
why_it_matters: Health insurance is one of the fastest-growing and most complained-about parts of Indian finance, so a new well-funded entrant can change choice, pricing and service. For buyers, a new insurer also means no track record on claims, so knowing what to check before buying matters more than the brand name.

title: MAS and Singapore's Banks Launch the ACT Taskforce to Counter AI-Driven Cyber Threats
summary: Announced on July 28, the AI-Driven Cyber and Technology Risk Taskforce brings the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the banking association, three local banks, the exchange and payment infrastructure operators together to share intelligence, test AI-enabled defences and draft guidance.
description:
Singapore's central bank and its banking association have created a joint taskforce to prepare the financial sector for cyber attacks that use advanced artificial intelligence. The Monetary Authority of Singapore and the Association of Banks in Singapore announced the AI-Driven Cyber and Technology Risk Taskforce, abbreviated as ACT, on July 28, 2026. The announcement was published in the press release carried by The Asian Banker on July 29, and discussed by other outlets including GRC Report.

Who is involved? The taskforce brings together the two convenors, MAS and ABS, with the three local banks DBS, OCBC and UOB, the Singapore Exchange, the Network for Electronic Transfers, known as NETS, and Banking Computer Services, known as BCS. That list is notable because it spans lenders, the stock exchange and the companies that run card and interbank payment infrastructure. Reports say the members combine expertise in cybersecurity, technology resilience and artificial intelligence, and that they have been working together since May 2026, so the July announcement formalised an effort that was already under way. The reports reviewed do not name a chair, give an end date or list publication deadlines.

What will it do? According to the press release, the work is organised around three focus areas. The first is industry collaboration. Members will share their use cases and experiences of applying AI to cybersecurity, and will engage outside cybersecurity and AI experts. The second is capability uplift. The group plans to build the sector's cyber defence knowledge and to run proof-of-concept trials that test advanced AI-enabled tools. The third is guidance. The taskforce intends to develop guidance on new measures, controls and solutions to detect, prevent and respond to AI-enabled threats. Detailed controls were not published at launch, so what banks will eventually be asked to do is not yet known.

Why now? Vincent Loy, MAS's assistant managing director for technology and its chief technology officer, said that frontier AI is increasing the severity, scale and sophistication of cyber threats, and that the sector needs to respond urgently and collaboratively. Ong-Ang Ai Boon, director of ABS, said AI is reshaping the cyber threat landscape and that close coordination, governance and partnership between regulators and industry will keep the sector resilient. GRC Report added context from a Bank for International Settlements bulletin published shortly before the launch. According to that coverage, the bulletin warned that frontier models can find vulnerabilities, build exploits and automate attack chains quickly and cheaply, which could favour attackers. If successful techniques spread at low cost, the article argues, defences built by each institution on its own become less effective.

To understand the concern, it helps to compare older and newer attacks. Traditionally, finding a weakness in a bank's software, writing code to exploit it and launching an attack required skilled people and a good deal of time, which limited how many attacks could be run at once. Advanced AI systems can reduce the effort for several of those steps, for example by scanning large amounts of code for errors, drafting convincing phishing messages or probing systems automatically. That does not mean every attack will succeed, but it can mean more attempts, made faster, by less experienced attackers. This is a general description of the risk that the officials cited, not a finding about any particular incident in Singapore.

The defensive side has the same potential. Banks already use machine-learning tools to spot fraud and unusual network activity, and newer systems may be able to triage alerts, review code for flaws and speed up the response to an incident. The proof-of-concept trials are intended to test which of these tools work in practice before they are relied on. Testing in a shared setting can help smaller members learn from larger ones, and it lets the regulator see what is effective before it writes expectations into supervisory guidance.

Why is a sector-wide approach sensible? Banks do not operate alone. A payment moves from a customer's bank through interbank networks and clearing systems, and securities trades pass through the exchange and its infrastructure. The inclusion of SGX, NETS and BCS in the taskforce reflects that dependence. A weakness in one link, or in a shared supplier, can affect many institutions at once. Sharing threat information early is one of the main ways a financial system can limit the damage from an attack that is spreading.

What does this mean for ordinary customers? In the short term, probably very little will change in how you use your account. The taskforce is about preparation, information sharing and guidance rather than new customer rules. The practical advice for individuals remains the same as before. Use the multi-factor authentication your bank offers, treat unexpected links and calls with suspicion, because AI can make scam messages more convincing, and report suspicious activity to your bank promptly. Banks and regulators can strengthen the system, but customers' habits still matter.

What should be watched next? The first test will be whether the taskforce publishes guidance and when. Industry guidance can influence supervisory expectations, so firms outside the taskforce, including smaller banks and fintech companies, may want to follow what it produces. It will also be worth watching whether further parties, such as insurers or other infrastructure operators, are invited to join. For now, the announcement is a statement of intent, backed by named participants and a work plan. It shows that Singapore's authorities treat AI-enabled cyber threats as a present risk to the financial sector and want banks to respond together rather than separately.
source_name: MAS and ABS (via The Asian Banker)
image_alt: Cybersecurity systems representing financial-sector technology resilience (illustrative)
key_points: The Monetary Authority of Singapore and the Association of Banks in Singapore announced the AI-Driven Cyber and Technology Risk Taskforce, known as ACT, on July 28, 2026.
Members are MAS, ABS, DBS, OCBC, UOB, Singapore Exchange, NETS and Banking Computer Services, and they have worked together informally since May 2026.

The work plan has three parts: industry collaboration, capability uplift through proof-of-concept trials of AI-enabled tools, and guidance on controls to detect, prevent and respond to AI-enabled threats.
MAS's chief technology officer Vincent Loy said frontier AI is increasing the severity, scale and sophistication of cyber threats; no end date or deliverable dates were published.
Coverage notes the launch followed a Bank for International Settlements bulletin warning that frontier models can find vulnerabilities and automate attack chains cheaply.
why_it_matters: Banks, payment networks and exchanges depend on each other, so a successful attack on one can spread to the others. A shared taskforce is meant to make the whole system harder to attack rather than leaving each institution to defend itself, which matters to anyone who banks, pays or invests in Singapore.

title: UAE Central Bank Law Transition Ended on September 16: What Banks, Insurers and Fintechs Now Face
summary: The one-year grace period under Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025 closed on September 16, and a law-firm newsletter reports the central bank granted no blanket extension; fines can reach AED 1 billion.
description:
The United Arab Emirates has moved from preparation to enforcement under its new central bank law. This article was first published in August, when financial institutions were counting down to a compliance deadline, and has been updated on October 13, 2026 now that the deadline has passed. Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025, issued on September 8, 2025 and published in the Official Gazette on September 15, 2025, repeals the 2018 central bank law and the 2023 decree-law on insurance activities and replaces them with one framework covering banking, insurance, other licensed financial institutions and financial market infrastructure. According to law firm Ashurst, affected entities had until September 16, 2026 to comply, and the Central Bank of the UAE could extend the period.

The key question after September 16 is whether any relief was granted. A newsletter from the UAE firm CMI & Co dated October 2 says the one-year transitional period closed on that date, that the law became fully enforceable with no transitional relief, and that the central bank confirmed no blanket extension had been granted. The same newsletter says enforcement against non-compliant entities began immediately. This is a single secondary source, so firms should verify their own position directly with the central bank or its published circulars rather than relying on a law firm's summary.

The penalties explain why firms took the deadline seriously. Ashurst and Hadef & Partners both report maximum administrative fines of AED 1 billion for licensed financial institutions and up to AED 5 million for authorised individuals. CMI & Co adds that the previous maximum for institutions was AED 200 million, which would make the new cap five times larger, but that comparison comes from one source. Fines can be collected by debiting accounts held with the central bank or with any licensed institution, and the central bank may publish its enforcement decisions, including the name of the violator. Conducting licensed financial activity without a licence is a criminal offence carrying imprisonment and substantial fines, and Hadef notes that marketing or promoting licensed services without authorisation is itself a regulated activity.

The law also redraws the perimeter of regulation. It extends beyond open banking to regulated data sharing across products such as wealth management, insurance, pensions and credit scoring. Payment services that use virtual assets are licensable, although the law carves out investment holdings and certain swaps. Technology providers whose platforms, applications, protocols or infrastructure facilitate financial services may fall under the central bank's oversight even if they have no direct dealings with customers. CMI & Co says that under Article 62 fintech platforms, API providers, payment infrastructure operators, open finance providers and decentralised platforms must either be licensed or hold a documented central bank opinion confirming that they are out of scope, and warns of criminal liability risk for operating without that clarity.

For insurers, the stakes are specific. CMI & Co says the transitional alignment period for insurers has closed and that insurers must now comply fully with Articles 78 to 106 and the implementing instruments, which cover capital adequacy, governance including board composition, independent actuarial functions and internal audit, claims-handling service levels, fraud prevention and outsourcing. It adds that insurance compliance gaps are now assessed within the same supervisory and enforcement framework as banking breaches. Separately, in May the central bank issued a remuneration regulation for banks and insurers, which, according to Pinsent Masons, applies to insurance and reinsurance companies for the first time and requires independent review of pay frameworks at least every three years.

Consumers gain new protections. The law requires licensed institutions to run anti-fraud systems, including strong authentication and transaction monitoring, and to disclose products transparently. It creates a unified, independent complaints authority covering banking and insurance, and specialised judicial committees to resolve financial disputes of up to AED 100,000, with decisions in disputes of that size not open to challenge. Compound interest on customer credit facilities is prohibited. The law also gives the central bank early-intervention powers over distressed institutions, from remedial capital or liquidity measures to replacing management, facilitating mergers, imposing moratoria and liquidation. Other provisions recognise the Digital Dirham as legal tender and make environmental, social and governance principles part of the central bank's statutory functions.

What should firms do? The practical steps suggested by law firms are to assess licensing status and regulatory classification, update governance, risk management and consumer protection frameworks, review technology and fintech models, align operations with the digital asset and ESG provisions, and engage with the central bank early. Fintech and technology providers should check whether they sit within the perimeter, because the cost of getting that wrong has risen sharply. Firms operating through free zones or without proper authorisation face particular scrutiny, according to legal advisers.

For customers and policyholders in the UAE, the change should be gradual rather than dramatic. If you have a complaint with a bank or insurer, you should expect a more unified process in time, but you should check the central bank's current guidance for how to file one. If you use a fintech app or payment service, check that it is licensed. The law is a long text, and details such as implementing circulars continue to emerge, so this article should be read as a summary of reported provisions rather than legal advice. Firms and individuals with specific obligations should read the decree-law itself and take advice from a qualified UAE lawyer.
key_points: Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025 was issued on September 8, 2025 and gazetted on September 15, 2025, replacing the 2018 central bank law and the 2023 insurance decree-law.
Affected firms had until September 16, 2026 to comply; the central bank could extend the period, and CMI & Co reports it confirmed that no blanket extension was granted.
Administrative fines can reach AED 1 billion for licensed institutions and AED 5 million for authorised individuals, and the central bank can publish violators' names and debit fines from accounts.
The law widens the regulatory perimeter to open finance, virtual-asset payment services and technology providers that facilitate financial services.
It creates a unified complaints authority for banking and insurance and specialised judicial committees for disputes of up to AED 100,000.
why_it_matters: Banks, insurers and fintechs operating in the UAE can no longer rely on transitional relief, and the penalties are large enough to affect boardroom priorities. Customers should also see a clearer route for complaints, while technology and fintech firms need to confirm whether they are now inside the regulator's perimeter.

title: AXA's First-Half 2026: Underlying EPS Up 8% to €2.19, Solvency II at 218%, and the 'Growing Forward' 2029 Plan That Followed on September 15
summary: AXA reported first-half 2026 underlying earnings per share of €2.19, up 8%, a Solvency II ratio of 218% and gross written premiums of €66.3 billion, then presented its 'Growing Forward' plan on September 15, 2026 targeting operating EPS growth of 7% to 9% a year and operating earnings after tax above €10 billion by 2029.
description:
AXA's first-half results for 2026 set up the plan the group presented two months later. The French insurer's half-year earnings release reports underlying earnings per share of €2.19, up 8% from the first half of 2025. Underlying earnings were €4.5 billion, up 4%, or up 9% excluding AXA IM, the asset management business that AXA sold to BNP Paribas on July 1, 2025. Excluding that disposal is the fairer comparison, because the sold business contributed to the prior-year figure and not to this year's.

By segment, property and casualty underlying earnings were €3.2 billion, up 6%, and life and health underlying earnings were €2.0 billion, up 11%. The release says AXA XL, its specialty unit, grew earnings by 4%, though it gives no absolute figure on the page. Gross written premiums and other revenues were €66.3 billion, up 5%: property and casualty premiums were €35.1 billion, up 3%, and life and health premiums were €31.2 billion, up 8%. Chief executive Thomas Buberl called the half "outstanding" and said AXA is an "all-weather company able to navigate changing market conditions," adding that "growth in Life increasingly balancing the growth in P&C." The estimated Solvency II ratio was 218% at June 30, 2026, up 3 points from January 1, 2026, after the removal of transitional grandfathering. The estimate includes a theoretical accrual for dividends and buybacks. Insurance Journal, reporting the results on July 31, gave net income of €4.2 billion, up 9%, and shareholders' equity of €44.7 billion, but those figures are not on the release page reviewed, so they are attributed to that report.

AXA said it expected 2026 underlying EPS growth at the upper end of its 6% to 8% target range under the "Unlock the Future" plan, and it said it would present its next plan for 2027 to 2029 on September 15, 2026, with roundtables with business chief executives on September 21.

On September 15, AXA presented "Growing Forward", with a horizon to 2029. According to ABC Bourse, which reported the main targets, AXA aims for average annual operating EPS growth of 7% to 9% over 2026 to 2029, up from 6% to 8% in the previous plan, and operating return on equity of 15% to 17% over 2027 to 2029, against 14% to 16% in the current plan. Book value per share is targeted to grow by about 15% a year on average over 2027 to 2029. The group targets operating earnings after tax above €10 billion by the end of the plan, compared with about €8.6 billion expected in 2026. ABC Bourse's article carries a correction clarifying that this is after tax, not before tax.

The plan sets out how cash will be handled. AXA targets about €25 billion of cumulative organic cash upstreaming from its businesses to the group over 2027 to 2029, compared with more than €21 billion targeted for 2023 to 2026. It will keep a stable total payout ratio of 75%, made up of 60% in dividends and 15% in share buybacks, and the dividend per share will be at least equal to the previous year's. Dividends and buybacks take priority over acquisitions. The group expects to keep a robust Solvency II ratio, supported by normalised operating capital generation of 25 to 30 points a year.

On growth, AXA aims for revenue growth above 5% a year over 2027 to 2029, one to two points above the market in its main segments, and for at least 100 million customers by the end of 2029, up from 92 million today. Growth areas named are savings and health, direct insurance, emerging markets and inclusive insurance. In property and casualty, the combined ratio is expected to stay stable at about 91% over the plan. A combined ratio below 100% means premiums exceed claims and costs, so a figure near 91% implies a wide underwriting margin that AXA intends to hold, not widen.

Artificial intelligence is a central theme. AXA says it will accelerate AI deployment across the value chain and estimates €500 million to €700 million in pre-tax recurring annual benefits by 2029. Buberl said the plan would also be one of accelerating AI deployment. Guillaume Borie, quoted by ABC Bourse, summed up the plan's ambition in a single word, "conquest", and the article says winning customers and market share is at the heart of it, though it gives no numerical market-share target.

Analysts' first reaction was measured. ABC Bourse quotes Jefferies as saying the new target represents a slight acceleration from the 6% to 8% of the previous plan. The article's page showed the share price at €42.89, down 0.72% when captured, but it does not state the price on the day of the announcement, so the market's verdict on the plan cannot be drawn from it.

These targets are management's ambitions and not guarantees. They depend on markets, catastrophe losses and execution. For exact definitions of operating and underlying measures, readers should consult AXA's own half-year release and the plan presentation.
source_name: AXA half-year 2026 earnings release, ABC Bourse (September 2026) and Insurance Journal (July 31, 2026)
image_alt: Corporate office building representing a global insurer's results (illustrative)
key_points: AXA's first-half 2026 underlying earnings per share were €2.19, up 8%; underlying earnings were €4.5 billion, up 4% or 9% excluding AXA IM, which was sold to BNP Paribas on July 1, 2025.

P&C underlying earnings were €3.2 billion (up 6%) and life and health €2.0 billion (up 11%); gross written premiums and other revenues were €66.3 billion, up 5%, and the Solvency II ratio was 218% at June 30, 2026.

On September 15, 2026 AXA presented 'Growing Forward' for 2027 to 2029, targeting average operating EPS growth of 7% to 9% (up from 6% to 8%), operating ROE of 15% to 17% and operating earnings after tax above €10 billion, against about €8.6 billion expected in 2026.

The plan targets about €25 billion of cumulative cash upstreaming in 2027-2029, a stable 75% total payout split 60% dividends and 15% buybacks, at least 100 million customers by end-2029 and a P&C combined ratio stable at about 91%.
AXA estimates €500 million to €700 million of pre-tax recurring annual benefits from AI by 2029; for 2026 it expects operating EPS growth at the upper end of 6% to 8%.
why_it_matters: AXA is one of Europe's largest insurers, so its targets show what a diversified group expects from pricing, savings, health and cost savings over the next three years. The step up in the EPS target from 6-8% to 7-9% is modest, and an analyst quoted by ABC Bourse described it as a slight acceleration. The numbers also show a shift in the mix of earnings, with life and health growing faster than property and casualty. For shareholders, the plan fixes how much of earnings is returned; for customers, the stated aim of 100 million customers and the AI savings target indicate where the company will invest.

title: Canadian Mortgage Stress Builds at Renewal as the Bank of Canada Holds at 2.25% and Warns of Upside Inflation Risks
summary: Equifax data show serious mortgage delinquencies rising from a low base and insolvencies at their highest since 2009, while the Bank of Canada held its rate at 2.25% on September 2 and said it is prepared to adjust policy as needed.
description:
The Bank of Canada kept its policy interest rate at 2.25% on September 2, 2026, and in doing so left Canadian mortgage borrowers in a mixed position. Rates are far below their recent peak, yet many homeowners are still renewing loans that were fixed when borrowing was much cheaper. Credit-bureau data suggest that the strain is showing up at the edges, in the most serious arrears and in insolvency filings, while the overall picture remains stable. This article explains what is known, with the source for each number.

Start with the central bank's decision. In its September 2 announcement the Bank of Canada held the overnight rate target at 2.25%, with the Bank Rate at 2.5% and the deposit rate at 2.20%. It said second-quarter GDP grew 3.3% after very weak growth in the first quarter, and that some of the strength was temporary even though the pickup was broad-based. Unemployment edged down to 6.4% in July, but demand for labour remains subdued and there is still excess supply in the economy. Consumer price inflation has been about 3% in recent months, mainly because of higher gasoline prices, while inflation excluding gasoline was 2.2% in July and core measures stayed close to 2%. The Bank said upside risks to inflation have increased, mainly because of the conflict in the Middle East and the possibility that higher energy costs spread to other prices, and that new United States tariffs and Canadian counter-tariffs could raise costs over time. Governing Council said it is prepared to adjust monetary policy as needed. The next rate announcement and Monetary Policy Report are scheduled for October 28, 2026.

That wording matters for mortgage holders. A central bank that says it is prepared to adjust policy as needed is not promising cuts, and it has pointed to risks that could push inflation up. For borrowers waiting for much lower rates before renewing, the Bank's own message is cautious.

Now turn to the borrowers. Equifax Canada's fourth-quarter 2025 data, reported by Canadian Mortgage Trends on March 16, 2026, put mortgage balances at about $2 trillion, up 2.6% on the year. The overall delinquency rate was low at 0.26%. However, severe delinquencies, meaning loans more than 90 days past due, rose 30% year on year by dollar value and nearly 15% by number of accounts. Ontario's delinquency rate rose above 0.3%. The increases were driven mainly by loans above $800,000, with the biggest rises in Ontario, British Columbia and Atlantic Canada. The pattern fits what lenders expect in a high-price market, where larger loans leave less room when payments rise.

The renewal cycle explains why this matters now. Equifax estimated that about 60% of outstanding mortgages would renew between 2025 and 2026, and that by the end of 2026 nearly a quarter of renewing borrowers would face higher payments as loans taken out during the period of very low rates reset. The source does not give a dollar figure for the typical payment increase, and the size of any increase depends on when the borrower locked in, the term chosen and today's rate. Borrowers who took five-year fixed loans at record-low rates in 2020 and 2021 are the group most exposed, while those who locked in later at higher rates may see smaller changes or even a lower payment.

Household debt more broadly shows the same tension. A Canadian Press report published by CTV News on May 26, 2026 said that insolvency volumes had reached their highest level since 2009, according to a new Equifax Canada report. Homeowner insolvencies rose by more than 11% from the fourth quarter of the previous year, and more than 90% of those homeowners chose consumer proposals rather than bankruptcy. Total consumer debt rose 4% year on year to $2.66 trillion. The report did not provide mortgage delinquency figures or an Ontario breakdown, so those numbers should not be inferred from it. A figure widely repeated earlier, that mortgage delinquency balances were up about 32% nationally and 52% in Ontario, could not be verified against the primary credit-bureau data in this review and has therefore been left out.

What can borrowers do? The practical steps are well known but worth stating. Check your renewal date well before it arrives, because lenders usually send an offer 60 to 120 days ahead, and shop the market rather than accepting the first offer, since a different lender may offer a lower rate. If payments will rise sharply, ask your lender about extending the amortization period, which lowers the payment at the cost of more interest over time, and consider whether a variable or shorter term fits your budget. Build a buffer for a rate increase, and speak to your lender early if you are struggling, because options are wider before a payment is missed. For insurance, remember that mortgage life and property insurance premiums are separate from your loan, so review them when you renew.

For lenders and regulators the issue is concentration. Stress that appears first among large loans in the most expensive markets, and among households that also carry other debts, is a signal to monitor rather than a sign of systemic trouble. The overall delinquency rate remains low, and the Bank of Canada's own assessment points to a recovering economy. The risk is that higher energy prices and trade tensions keep inflation above target and delay the relief that borrowers hope for.

The next data points to watch are the Bank of Canada's October 28 decision and the next quarterly Equifax report. Anyone reading headlines should check whether a figure refers to balances, accounts or rates, and whether it describes arrears or insolvency, because the numbers measure different things. The borrower's own renewal date and budget remain the most useful information for personal decisions.
image_alt: House keys and documents representing mortgage renewal stress (illustrative)
key_points: On September 2, 2026 the Bank of Canada held its overnight rate target at 2.25%, with the Bank Rate at 2.5% and the deposit rate at 2.20%; the next decision is October 28.
The Bank said CPI inflation has been about 3% in recent months, mainly because of gasoline, while inflation excluding gasoline was 2.2% in July.
Equifax Canada data for late 2025 show the overall mortgage delinquency rate at 0.26%, but severe delinquencies more than 90 days past due rose 30% by dollar value.
Equifax estimated about 60% of outstanding mortgages renew between 2025 and 2026, and nearly one-quarter of renewing borrowers could face higher payments by the end of 2026.
Equifax reported in May 2026 that insolvency volumes were the highest since 2009, and that more than 90% of homeowners who became insolvent chose consumer proposals over bankruptcy.
why_it_matters: Most Canadian mortgages are renewed every few years, so changes in interest rates reach households in waves rather than at once. Understanding where the Bank of Canada stands and how many borrowers are renewing helps homeowners plan, and shows lenders and regulators where stress could appear first.
